input: This passage explains the pump affinity laws, which describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its rotational speed is varied, and it is worth working through them carefully because they are simple, powerful and widely used. In essence, the affinity laws consist of three proportionalities. First, the volumetric flow rate is directly proportional to the speed: if the speed is increased, the flow increases in exactly the same proportion. Second, the head is proportional to the square of the speed, so the head rises much more steeply as the speed goes up. Third, the power is proportional to the cube of the speed, rising more steeply still. A worked check makes the point concrete. When the speed is doubled, that is, increased by a factor of 2, the flow is multiplied by 2, the head is multiplied by 4 and the power is multiplied by 8. The power figure is the one that most often surprises people, highlighting just how strongly the energy demand responds to a speed change, and it explains why even a modest speed reduction can deliver a substantial saving, while a modest speed increase can overload a motor that appeared to have ample margin. It should be noted that these proportionalities apply to one and the same pump running at different speeds, with the impeller diameter unchanged and the same liquid being pumped, and they rest on the assumption that the efficiency stays broadly constant across the change, which is reasonable for moderate speed changes but becomes less secure as the change grows larger. Used within those limits, the laws let you move a known duty point to a new speed quickly and with confidence, without repeating a full pump test.
target: The affinity laws give the duty of a centrifugal pump at a new speed from a known duty: doubling the speed doubles the flow, multiplies the head fourfold and multiplies the power eightfold. The laws are three proportionalities for one pump at varying speed, with the impeller diameter and the liquid unchanged. Flow is proportional to speed. Head is proportional to the square of the speed. Power is proportional to the cube of the speed. In symbols, $Q$ varies with $N$, $H$ with $N$ squared and $P$ with $N$ cubed, where $Q$ denotes the volumetric flow rate, $H$ the head, $P$ the shaft power and $N$ the rotational speed. The three proportionalities have one source. The impeller tip speed rises in direct proportion to $N$, and the flow through the pump follows the tip speed. The energy imparted to each unit weight of liquid follows the square of the tip speed, and head is that energy stated per unit weight. Power is flow multiplied by head, and a quantity that follows $N$ multiplied by a quantity that follows $N$ squared gives a quantity that follows $N$ cubed. The worked check follows directly. A speed increase by a factor of 2 multiplies the flow by 2, because the flow follows the speed itself. The same increase multiplies the head by 4, because the head follows the square. The power rises by 8, because the power follows the cube. The power term carries the practical weight of the check: a speed rise that looks small against the flow gain raises the power demand eightfold at a doubling, and a motor sized close to the original duty is overloaded well before the flow gain is reached. The proportionalities rest on the efficiency staying constant across the speed change. Affinity laws hold for moderate speed changes around the known duty; at large changes the efficiency moves, and the predicted duty is an estimate to be confirmed against the pump curve.
